title: LLM Reliability: Hallucination, Evaluation, Cost and Safety
summary: Quick revision notes on why LLMs hallucinate, how grounding and citations reduce it, how to evaluate outputs (benchmarks, LLM-as-judge, human eval), which latency and cost metrics matter, and safety basics.

chapters.title: Why Models Hallucinate
points: Hallucination = fluent output that is false or unsupported by the source; the model predicts likely next tokens, not verified facts
Causes: gaps or errors in training data, rare or long-tail facts, and knowledge cutoff (no data after a date)
Intrinsic hallucination contradicts the provided context; extrinsic adds claims that cannot be verified from it
Training rewards confident guessing over saying 'I don't know', so models rarely abstain without prompting
Mistake: assuming a lower temperature removes hallucination; it only makes output more deterministic, not more true

chapters.title: Grounding and Citations
points: Grounding = forcing answers to rest on supplied sources (RAG, tool/API results, database lookups) instead of model memory
Core workflow: retrieve top-k chunks, put them in the prompt, instruct 'answer only from the context', else say 'not found'
Citations: tag each claim with a source ID or chunk quote so a reader or program can verify it
Verify citations programmatically: check the cited ID exists and the quoted span actually appears in the source
Mistake: a citation proves nothing alone; models can cite real sources that do not support the claim, and bad retrieval gives confident wrong answers

chapters.title: Evaluation Methods
points: Benchmarks give cheap, reproducible, comparable scores (classic MMLU, HumanEval and GSM8K are now saturated at ~90%+, and their harder successors MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond are nearing saturation too, so use fresher, harder benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam or SWE-bench Pro to separate current models) but suffer contamination and may not match your task
LLM-as-judge: a strong model scores outputs against a rubric; it scales cheaply but shows position bias, verbosity bias and self-preference
Human eval is the gold standard for nuance and safety but is slow and costly; measure inter-annotator agreement (e.g. Cohen's kappa)
Build a golden set of 50-200 real task examples with expected answers and run it on every prompt or model change
Mistake: relying on public benchmark rank alone; also unvalidated judges, so calibrate the judge against human labels and swap answer order

chapters.title: Latency and Cost Metrics
points: Latency metrics: TTFT (time to first token, drives perceived speed), inter-token latency, and total latency = TTFT + tokens x per-token time
Throughput = tokens/sec or requests/sec; track p50 and p95/p99 latency, not just the average
Cost = input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price; output tokens usually cost several times more than input
Levers: smaller model for easy tasks, prompt caching for repeated prefixes, shorter prompts, max_tokens cap, batching for offline jobs, streaming for UX
Mistake: optimizing average cost per call and ignoring cost per successful task; retries, long contexts and agent loops multiply spend

chapters.title: Safety Basics
points: Prompt injection: untrusted text (web page, email, document) carries instructions that hijack the model; indirect injection is the common real-world form
Defenses are layered: separate trusted instructions from untrusted data, least-privilege tools, confirm destructive actions, and sandbox execution
Input and output guardrails: moderation or classifier filters, PII redaction, schema validation of outputs, refusal handling
Never put secrets in prompts; treat model output as untrusted input before it touches a shell, SQL or HTML (injection risk)
Mistake: trusting 'ignore malicious instructions' in the system prompt as the only defense; add red-teaming and logging of flagged cases

chapters.title: LLM Reliability Cheat Sheet
points: Hallucination fixes: ground with retrieval, require citations, allow 'not found', verify claims
Eval stack: golden set for regressions, benchmark for model choice, calibrated LLM-judge for scale, human review for high stakes
Latency: TTFT for feel, p95 for reliability; cost = input and output tokens x price
Cost levers: smaller model, prompt caching, token caps, batching
Safety: assume injection, least privilege, validate outputs, redact PII, red-team
